newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New U.N. chief Annan wants reform and money.
newsitem.headline: New U.N. chief Annan wants reform and money.

text.p: Kofi Annan, the 58-year old Ghanaian and new U.N. secretary-general, began his first day of work on Thursday as the world's top diplomat and immediately pledged to reform the United Nations.

At the same time Annan, who was greeted by an honour guard of U.N. police and cheering onlookers, said he expected member states to honour their commitments to the world organisation, a veiled reference to the more than $2 billion owed to the United Nations, most of it from the United States.
"This is my first day. It is like the first day in school. Everyone expects a lot from you and you get into it with considerable trepidation," he told the crowd.

U.N. officials said he had spoken to President Bill Clinton shortly after being sworn in by the U.N. General Assembly on Dec. 17 and was invited to come to Washington as soon as he was able, possibly this month.

Annan already has an invitation from Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, to discuss his plans before the committee in an effort to break the funding logjam, on which the success of his term largely depends.
"The member states have made it clear that they want changes and they have given us unanimous support," Annan said.

"And I think together we can achieve a lot, bring about the reforms that are necessary, encourage the member states to work together, to honour their commitment to the organisation and together make the changes that are required if we are to make the United Nations as relevant as it ought to be as we move into the 21st century," he added.
His spokesman Fred Eckhard, an American, said Annan intended to press member states immediately on setting priorities and then arranging his administration accordingly.

"His first job is nailing down governments of some essential agreement on what the work of this organisation is to be. This means establishing priorities and then re-arranging the administration to do that job. and adjusting the finances."

Eckhard said the United Nations had spent 10 years considering various reports on reform. "It is time now to make a decision and he would like that decision to be made in the early days of his administration," he said.
Flanked by his new team, mainly from the peacekeeping department he headed, Annan went to the office occupied by Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt for the past five years and shook hands with his staff.
"Okay, now we go to work," he said, putting on his spectacles and leafing through the first set of documents.
The gray-bearded soft-spoken Annan, who was the undersecretary-general for peacekeeping operations, is the seventh U.S. secretary-general.
He is also the first from sub-Saharan Africa and the first to have risen through the ranks of the U.N. bureaucracy.
He succeeds the 74-year-old Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, to the $205,809-a-year post for the next five years.

He and his wife Nane, a Swedish lawyer and artist, moved from their flat on Roosevelt Island in the East River to a hotel in Manhattan while the secretary-general's house on elegant Sutton Place was being renovated.
Boutros-Ghali left for his home of Cairo on Tuesday and intends to live in France for several months to write a book on his years in the United Nations.
The United States, a supporter of Annan, orchestrated Boutros-Ghali's ouster, blocking his hopes for a second term by vetoing his candidacy in November.

In saying he had not done enough to carry out reforms and that the world organisation needed new leadership, the Clinton administration is facing pressure from its allies and foes alike to pay the outstanding $1.3 billion for dues and peacekeeping to the United Nations.
But so far the Republican-dominated Congress has shown few signs it is willing to pay the arrears quickly.
At one point Marc Thiessen, the spokesman for Helms, spoke of a 50 percent reduction in U.N. staff rather than the 10 percent Boutros-Ghali initiated.

Many Congressmen also believe the United States is contributing disproportionately to the United Nations in both dues and voluntary contributions, although most European countries and Japan pay more in relation to their income.
